content_voiceover: We now shift topics to von Willebrand disease, and this slide illustrates the classic mucocutaneous bleeding pattern. You see bruising and ecchymoses on the thigh, an image referencing menorrhagia or heavy menstrual bleeding, and two photos of oral and gingival bleeding. This mucocutaneous pattern, bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction or minor cuts, is the hallmark of a primary hemostasis defect, whether that's a platelet disorder or von Willebrand disease, in contrast to the deep muscle and joint bleeding, hemarthroses, seen in factor deficiencies like hemophilia, which reflect a secondary hemostasis or coagulation factor problem. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting roughly one percent of the population, though clinically significant disease is much less common. For boards, always link the bleeding phenotype to the pathophysiology, mucocutaneous equals platelet-type or VWF problem, deep tissue equals clotting factor problem, and menorrhagia is often the presenting symptom that brings women with VWD to medical attention.
keypoints: Mucocutaneous bleeding: bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia
Pattern reflects a primary hemostasis defect (platelet/VWF), not deep tissue bleeding
VWD = most common inherited bleeding disorder (~1% prevalence)
Menorrhagia is often the presenting symptom in women
keypoint_voiceover: Von Willebrand disease classically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, bruising, gum bleeding, epistaxis, and menorrhagia, reflecting a primary hemostasis defect rather than the deep joint and muscle bleeding seen in factor deficiencies. It is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting about one percent of people, and menorrhagia is frequently the symptom that leads to diagnosis in women.
